source.title: Double Descent in Quantum Kernel Ridge Regression
source.authors: Kensuke Kamisoyama; Lento Nagano; K. Terashi

record.tranche_reason: Tests double descent in quantum kernel ridge regression, a quantum-model setting, using a sample-size sweep and regularization comparisons.
record.gate_note: The study varies training sample count and reports empirical test-error curves and deterministic-equivalent predictions. Cited results from earlier work are not included. The theoretical argument and Figure 6–7 curves are included as results; exact curve values are not stated in the text.
record.test_reason: The study gives its own empirical test-error curves for quantum kernel ridge regression (HEA and TPA circuits). Each sweep varies the training sample count Ntr at fixed effective dimension p and five ridge values. It reports a peak at Ntr = p that regularization suppresses. It also derives a deterministic-equivalent theory that places the peak where the normalized effective degrees of freedom ηλ approach 1 and traces it to the variance term. This is a new (quantum kernel) setting with results on V3, V5 and V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors derive a rigorous fixed-λ deterministic equivalent for QKRR test risk that captures the double-descent peak at p = Ntr. They attribute the peak to divergence of the variance term as ηλ → 1 and show that explicit regularization suppresses it. Numerics show close agreement even at 3 and 5 qubits, improving with effective dimension and strongest for HEA. Fashion-MNIST is only a robustness check with calibrated σ. The second dip and vanishing-regularization regimes are left to future work.
record.recipe_differences: Quantum kernel ridge regression with fixed quantum feature maps and explicit ridge regularization; evaluates test error while varying sample count and compares it with an RMT deterministic equivalent, rather than reproducing deep-network model-size or epoch sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported peak and its magnitude vary with regularization λ; the study also compares HEA with TPA and synthetic teacher–student data with Fashion-MNIST. It reports closer theory–empirics agreement at larger effective feature dimension.

fits_no_version.finding: The agreement between the deterministic-equivalent prediction and the empirical test error improves with effective feature dimension (HEA 5-qubit, p = 1024, closest; TPA 5-qubit, p = 243, less so).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Random-matrix deterministic equivalents predict the shape and height of the double-descent peak in small quantum kernel models, and their accuracy grows with effective dimension.

record.problems: Exact curve values and uncertainty intervals are not stated in the text; the plotted comparisons are reported as figures. The Fashion-MNIST noise parameter is calibrated to match at λ = 10^-2, and the authors say the theorem's assumptions cannot be verified for that dataset. Experiments use 3- and 5-qubit circuits; no model-size or epoch-wise sweep is performed.

untested.parts: No model-size sweep; p is fixed per circuit (n = 3, 5 qubits only, not swept densely).
No training-time axis; closed-form kernel ridge solution; epoch-wise double descent is named as future work.
Only kernel ridge regression with fixed quantum feature maps; no deep networks or iterative training; whether more data hurts under strong regularization is not quantified.
Experiments vary Ntr at fixed p rather than capacity, so the post-threshold descent is over decreasing sample count, not growing capacity; no comparison across model classes.
The ηλ account is shown only for the sample-size axis. No test that one complexity measure locates peaks along model-size or epoch axes.
Label-noise level is fixed (σ = 0.3 synthetic); no noise sweep. No test for multiple or triple peaks. No optimally tuned λ, so disappearance of the peak under optimal regularization is not shown.
No re-plotting against an effective parameter count showing the second descent becomes U-shaped.

missing.what: Plot of the normalized effective DOF ηλ vs γ̃ for the 3-qubit synthetic HEA, showing ηλ approaching 1 near the interpolation threshold at small λ. This is the empirical-side evidence for V5's peak-location claim.
Small-λ asymptotics: 1/(1−η) diverges only at γ̃ = 1 and stays finite for γ̃ < 1 and γ̃ > 1. In the overparameterized regime an implicit ridge κ0 > 0 acts even when λ → 0.

record.verdict_notes: All empirical rows are figure-only, with no numbers or error bars stated in the text. The study varies samples at fixed p, so its x-axis 'model complexity ratio' p/Ntr is a sample-wise sweep, not a capacity sweep. This is why V4 and V1 are left untested. The V5 and V6 verdicts rely on theory (R31) plus Fig. 11, not on independent empirical manipulations. Neither original source is this study.

versions.untested_parts: No controlled sweep of model size with test error measured as model size grows.
No epoch- or training-time sweep; the conclusion identifies epoch-wise double descent as future work.
Tested by varying sample size for fixed feature dimensions and quantum circuits; not tested across other training procedures or model families.
The study tests QKRR, but its empirical sweeps vary sample size at fixed feature dimension rather than capacity across model classes.
The effective-degrees-of-freedom account is analyzed for the sample-size/interpolation setting only, not for model-size or epoch-wise peaks.

Regularization suppression and the variance contribution to the peak are analyzed. The study does not vary label-noise level, test for multiple or triple peaks, or tune regularization optimally to establish disappearance.
No comparison shows that counting complexity by effective parameters converts a second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: QKRR deterministic-equivalent analysis
rows.size_stated: effective feature dimension p; proportional regime p/Ntr → γ ∈ (0, ∞)
rows.operation_detail: Derived a deterministic equivalent for test risk and analyzed its effective degrees of freedom and variance term.

conditions.value: fixed λ > 0 for theorem; λ ↓ 0 analyzed at fixed finite p and Ntr

rows.measure: Test-risk deterministic equivalent; normalized second-order effective degrees of freedom ηλ
rows.value: The variance term is σ²ηλ/(1 − ηλ); at p = Ntr, as λ ↓ 0, 1 − ηλ ∝ √λ and the variance contribution grows as λ^-1/2. The peak is associated with ηλ approaching 1.
rows.locator: Theorem 1; Section III B; Appendices I and J
rows.note: The analysis links peak behavior to effective degrees of freedom for the sample-size axis. It does not test a single predictor across model-size and epoch axes or vary noise levels.
rows.check: The state was set to partial because other axes (size, epochs) are untested, but untested axes belong under untested, not in the row state. Within the sample-size axis, the theory places the peak exactly where ηλ→1 at p = Ntr and assigns the divergence to the variance term σ²ηλ/(1−ηλ). This is an analytic result, not an empirical measurement, and it is backed by Fig. 11 and by close agreement with the empirical curves.

source_check.locator_found: Theorem 1, Equations (56–57); Section III B, Equation (63); Appendix J.2, Equations (J27–J30); Appendix L, Figure 11.

relationships.display_finding: Test error peaks at Ntr=p, so adding samples just below p increases error.
